text.p: Singapore has relaxed its tough anti-smoking rules for the WTO conference.
By law, there is no smoking in any building with air-conditioning, and offenders can be fined up to Singapore $1,000 (US$715).
Throwing cigarette butts anywhere but in a public ashtray can also bring grief -- for repeat offenders it can mean being sentenced to street cleaning duties.
But police said they have relaxed the rule in the huge convention centre where the 128 member countries of the World Trade Organisation are holding their first ministerial meeting.
Smoking remains banned in the auditorium and media centre. But it is permitted in the corridors.
Tall ashtrays have been provided for the desperate delegates and reporters who still cling to old comforts that space-age Singapore has left behind.
Many stores in Singapore are rubbing their hands at thoughts of the business to be had from WTO delegates and camp followers.
However, for around 40 shops the climax of the week-long event will be, in the words of one owner, "a pain that'll cost me money".

The closing ceremony will be held on Friday on the island of Sentosa, off the main Singapore island, and stores and restaurants there have been told to close for half a day. They were given no reason.
Sentosa is Singapore's most popular tourist spot with funfair rides and other attractions.
Two storeowners told Reuters they had been offered no compensation.
To add insult to injury, the closed premises must leave their lights on until midnight.
Officials on Sentosa declined to comment.
The wealthy city state is laying on a fleet of 200 new BMW 728i cars and drivers for the ministers.
A local BMW agent is providing them free and will sell them after the conference at a nine percent discount.
Several international stars will entertain the ministers and their delegation members -- some 4,000 of them -- on Friday the 13th, when the conference ends.
Among them are Lea Salonga -- star of the musical "Miss Saigon" when it opened in London -- who will perform with five Singaporean child musicians and dancers.
Shirley Bassey, the Welsh-born singer whose career just goes on and on, will be there to perform "Goldfinger", which has become her signature song.
So will Sarah Brightman, former wife of composer Andrew Lloyd Webber and star of his "Phantom of the Opera".
Hindi-language pop star Sharon Prabhakar will also perform -- along with 15 dancers.
The WTO offers glimpses of a vanishing breed, Gurkha soldiers.
Singapore is one of the last employers of the tough Nepalis, who have been at the cutting edge of many of the British Empire's toughest battles.
Their other major foreign residence in Asia, Hong Kong, is lost to them as the British colony reverts to China in mid-1997.
The Nepalis' ordinary duties in Singapore include guarding prisons and the homes of prominent politicians.
Wearing their familiar broad-rim ranger-style hats they are now helping guard the conference.
